subject: mathematics
question_text: If A + B + C = π/2, show that sin 2A + sin 2B + sin 2C = 4 cos A cos B cos C.

mark_split.label: Pair two terms and expand the third
Apply the sum formula and conclude

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), the TRANSFORMATIONS banner (the book prints TRANSFORMATIONS as a separate un-numbered chapter-style banner immediately after chapter 8's VSAQ run, and restarts its numbering at 1 — we ship both under one unit, ordered by the syllabus, and never mirror the book's arrangement), Long Answer question 5(ii), book p.101. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The split gives two marks each to the three moves that carry the proof — the pairing, the substitution from the π/2 condition, and the factoring that uses the condition a second time — with one mark for the set-up and one for the finish. THE CONDITION IS π/2, NOT π: A + B = π/2 − C gives sin(A+B) = cos C, whereas the triangle version would give sin(A+B) = +sin C and produce a product of sines instead of cosines. The right-hand side of this question is a product of COSINES, which is the visible sign that the π/2 condition is the one in use. NUMERIC CHECK (before authoring and again after): at A = 30°, B = 25°, C = 35°, which sums to 90°, L.H.S = 2.5717624677 and R.H.S = 2.5717624677. The printed identity is correct as stated. Paper position: Maths-1A Section C prints 3 long answers and the student answers any 2, at 8 marks each (2026-27 pattern). This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this identity — say the four moves in order, and where the angle condition gets used.

steps.label: State the π/2 condition
steps.margin_note: First mark. The condition here is π/2, not π. Write it as A + B = π/2 − C, the form step 3 needs.
steps.memory_tip: The sum is π/2 here, not π. The answer is a product of COSINES, and only the π/2 condition can produce cosines.
lines: The sum is π/2 here, not π.

recall.must_convey: That the condition is A + B + C = π/2 and it is rearranged to A + B = π/2 − C.
accept: the sum is pi by two so A plus B equals pi by two minus C
write the condition first and rearrange it
state the angle condition, and note it is pi by two not pi
modata condition rasi, A plus B ni pi by two minus C ga rayali
write down the given sum in the form the proof needs

steps.why: The statement is false without the condition, and false with the wrong one. Writing A + B = π/2 − C now fixes the sign of every substitution below.
common_mistakes: Using A + B = π − C, which is the triangle condition and gives sines on the right.
Starting the transformation before writing the condition.

steps.label: Pair two terms
steps.margin_note: Two of the eight marks. Three terms will not factorise as they stand, so the first two are combined into a product and the third is opened by the double angle formula.
steps.memory_tip: Pair sin 2A with sin 2B, and open sin 2C as 2 sin C cos C so both parts carry cos C.
lines: [∵ sin p + sin q = 2 sin((p+q)/2) cos((p−q)/2)]

recall.must_convey: That sin 2A + sin 2B becomes 2 sin(A+B) cos(A−B), and sin 2C is opened as 2 sin C cos C.
accept: pair the first two with the sin C plus sin D formula and open sin two C as two sin C cos C
apply sum to product on the first pair and the double angle on the third
combine two of the terms and expand the other one
modati rendu terms ni sum to product cheyyali, moodava term double angle
use sinC plus sinD on the first pair

steps.why: Three terms cannot be factorised as they stand. Pairing two makes a product, and opening the third gives it the cos C that the pair will end up sharing.
common_mistakes: Trying to expand all three terms at once.
Pairing sin 2B with sin 2C, which leaves nothing in common.

steps.label: Use the condition
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. Under the π/2 condition a SINE of (A+B) becomes a COSINE of C. That is what makes both terms carry cos C.
steps.memory_tip: sin(π/2 − C) = cos C. A sine becomes a cosine under a π/2 shift.

recall.must_convey: That A + B = π/2 − C gives sin(A+B) = cos C, so both terms now carry cos C.
accept: A plus B is pi by two minus C so its sine is cos C
sin of pi by two minus C is cos C
use the condition so both terms carry cos C
A plus B ante pi by two minus C, daani sin cos C
apply the angle condition to the sin A plus B term

steps.why: The right-hand side is a product of three cosines, so the compound sine has to become a cosine. Only the π/2 condition does that; the triangle condition would leave a sine.
common_mistakes: Using sin(π − C) = sin C, which belongs to the triangle version of this question.

steps.label: Take the common factor out
steps.margin_note: Two marks. 2 cos C comes out, and the condition is used a SECOND time inside the bracket so that both bracket terms are cosines. Only the inside sin C converts.
steps.memory_tip: Take 2 cos C out, then write the sin C inside the bracket as cos(A+B).

recall.must_convey: That 2 cos C is taken out and the sin C inside the bracket is rewritten as cos(A+B).
accept: take two cos C common then write the sin C inside the bracket as cos A plus B
factor out two cos C and convert the sine using the condition again
the bracket becomes cos A minus B plus cos A plus B
two cos C common teesi, bracket lo sin C ni cos A plus B ga marchali
use the condition a second time inside the bracket

steps.why: The condition is used twice — once outside on the compound sine, once inside on sin C. Both bracket terms must be cosines before a product formula applies.
common_mistakes: Converting the cos C outside as well, which cancels the factor just taken out.
Taking out cos C instead of 2 cos C.

steps.label: Apply the sum formula
steps.margin_note: Last mark. cos(A−B) + cos(A+B) = 2 cos A cos B closes the proof. Write "= R.H.S" so the examiner can see it landed.
steps.memory_tip: cos(A−B) + cos(A+B) = 2 cos A cos B. The two 2s multiply to give the 4.

recall.must_convey: That cos(A−B) + cos(A+B) = 2 cos A cos B, giving 4 cos A cos B cos C.
accept: cos A minus B plus cos A plus B is two cos A cos B so the answer is four cos A cos B cos C
the bracket becomes two cos A cos B and closes the proof
apply the cosine sum formula to finish
bracket lo two cos A cos B vasthundi, rendu twos kalisi four
the final answer is four cos A cos B cos C
heard_as: four cos A cos B cos C

steps.why: The sum of two cosines is a product of two cosines. The 4 comes from the 2 taken out in step 4 times the 2 this formula supplies.
common_mistakes: Using the cosine DIFFERENCE formula, which gives 2 sin A sin B.
Writing 2 cos A cos B cos C and losing one factor of 2.
